items.summary: Introduction Acupuncture at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) alleviates postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Nevertheless, the central regulatory effects of PC6 stimulation on virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), a form of physiological vertigo triggered by visual-vestibular sensory conflict, and the corresponding alterations in electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate characteristics remain unclear. Advances in stimulation strategies, molecular tools, functional materials and neural interfaces have progressively expanded the precision and versatility of such interventions. items.summary: Introduction Neuromodulatory interventions can produce overlapping adaptive outcomes despite engaging substantially different biological pathways. Pathway-centered approaches identify how interventions initially engage the nervous system and characterize pathway-specific mechanisms. Convergence across interventions raises an additional question: how can different biological routes influence overlapping domains of adaptive function? items.summary: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). items.summary: Binary P300 decoding is a cornerstone of P300-based brain-computer interfaces, enabling applications such as assistive communication, neurorehabilitation, and cognitive monitoring. However, substantial subject variability in EEG patterns poses a major challenge to the development of generalized P300 decoders. To address this problem, this study proposes SQ_EMoE, a subject-variability-aware enhanced Mixture-of-Experts framework that uses the confidence produced by a deep subject-identification network as a practical proxy for trial-level subject distinctiveness. items.summary: Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of distributed neural dynamics. Resting-state fMRI combined with signal-complexity measures may provide new insights into alterations in spontaneous brain activity. This study investigated whether weighted permutation entropy (WPE), an amplitude-sensitive measure of temporal complexity, could identify regional abnormalities in AD and characterize their temporal and network-level features. items.summary: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a clinical syndrome primarily affecting cognitive functions such as learning, memory, perception, and problem-solving. Its causes are heterogeneous, including neurological, psychiatric, metabolic, vascular, toxicological, and age-related factors. Currently, no specific and effective pharmacological therapies are available for CI in clinical practice. As one of the most abundant dietary polyphenols, chlorogenic acid (CGA) displays diverse biological effects and has recently garnered growing interest within cognitive neuroscience. Inspired by predictive coding mechanisms in neuroscience, this paper proposes a spatiotemporal joint representation framework driven by brain-like visual attention. We identified a "salience network," anchored by dorsal anterior cingulate (dACC) and orbital frontoinsular cortices with robust connectivity to subcortical and limbic structures, and an "executive-control network" that links dorsolateral frontal and parietal neocortices. items.summary: Correlation coefficient is widely used in biomedical and biological literature. Yet, its frequent misuse and misinterpretation undermine the credibility and reproducibility of the scientific findings. items.summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows marked interindividual variation that complicates efforts to identify coherent neuroanatomical signatures. Here we combine subject-wise morphometric-similarity networks with hierarchical Bayesian normative regression to map per-region, per-subject departures from expected cortical organization across 308 parcels in a large multisite cohort. Normative z-maps reveal that ASD individuals have a higher prevalence of extreme, spatially focal deviations than controls, yet fewer than 12% of cases show extreme deviation in any single region. items.summary: This treatise undertakes a comprehensive and critically systematic reconstruction of what is known about human learning and the person who learns. Its central premise is that the age-old division between theories of learning and conceptions of the learner is artificial: every theory of learning implicitly embodies a model of the learner, and every adequate model of the learner presupposes specific commitments regarding how learning occurs. items.summary: Kallmann syndrome (KS) arises from impaired development of the olfactory–GnRH neuronal system, yet the molecular consequences of individual gene defects remain poorly defined. In particular, the link between primary genetic variants and downstream transcriptional changes affecting neurodevelopmental pathways remains poorly understood. In the present study, we analyzed a Polish family with X-linked KS. We identified a hemizygous ANOS1 variant (c.452G > C; p.Cys151Ser) in two affected brothers presenting with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and olfactory impairment. The identified ANOS1 variant re

items.summary: Background Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Early prediction for clinical outcomes is essential for guiding therapy. Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers detailed characterization of ischemic tissue and may predict prognosis in AIS patients. This study assesses the prognostic value of multiparametric MRI parameters in predicting functional outcome, recurrence risk and mortality in AIS patients. Contemporary classrooms are characterized by significant cognitive, linguistic, cultural and motivational diversity, which poses new challenges for teachers. Traditional approaches to foreign language teaching, based on uniform methods of content presentation and standardized forms of student activity may limit learners’ participation in the learning process. The aim of the study is to present the theoretical and practical foundations

In the most used animal model of menopause, ovariectomized young adult rats, prolame produces estrogenic and antidepressant-like effects, making it a potential alternative to conventional ERT. A previous study indicated that aging cancels out the antidepressant-like effect of estradiol and reduces the window of antidepressant action of prolame, limiting it to only 3 weeks after ovariectomy. items.summary: Gut microbiome dysbiosis has been proposed as an Alzheimer’s disease (AD) biomarker, but the transportability of microbiome classifiers across independent cohorts remains uncertain. We reprocessed five public 16S rRNA cohorts (509 samples, China, Kazakhstan, South Korea) with a common DADA2/genus-level pipeline and evaluated logistic regression and LightGBM classifiers using nested within-cohort cross-validation, leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) transfer, pairwise transfer, permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), batch adjustment, and out-of-fold SHapley Additive exPlanations (

items.title: Global, regional, and national incidence, prevalence, and years lived with disability for 328 diseases and injuries for 195 countries, 1990–2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016
items.summary: BACKGROUND: As mortality rates decline, life expectancy increases, and populations age, non-fatal outcomes of diseases and injuries are becoming a larger component of the global burden of disease. The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2016 (GBD 2016) provides a comprehensive assessment of prevalence, incidence, and years lived with disability (YLDs) for 328 causes in 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2016. METHODS: We estimated prevalence and incidence for 328 diseases and injuries and 2982 sequelae, their non-fatal consequences. We used DisMod-MR 2.1, a Baye

items.title: FieldTrip: Open Source Software for Advanced Analysis of MEG, EEG, and Invasive Electrophysiological Data
items.summary: This paper describes FieldTrip, an open source software package that we developed for the analysis of MEG, EEG, and other electrophysiological data. The software is implemented as a MATLAB toolbox and includes a complete set of consistent and user-friendly high-level functions that allow experimental neuroscientists to analyze experimental data. It includes algorithms for simple and advanced analysis, such as time-frequency analysis using multitapers, source reconstruction using dipoles, distributed sources and beamformers, connectivity analysis, and nonparametric statistical permutation tests

items.title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
items.summary: BACKGROUND: The quality and quantity of individuals' social relationships has been linked not only to mental health but also to both morbidity and mortality. OBJECTIVES: This meta-analytic review was conducted to determine the extent to which social relationships influence risk for mortality, which aspects of social relationships are most highly predictive, and which factors may moderate the risk. ImageJ is in the public domain and runs on any operating system (OS). ImageJ is easy to use and can do many imaging manipulations. A very large and knowledgeable group makes up the user community for ImageJ. Topics covered are imaging abilities; cross platform; image formats support as of June 2004; extensions, including macros and plug-ins; and imaging library. NIH report

Despite its conceptual simplicity and broad applicability, it is rarely integrated into the undergraduate physics curriculum. We present the Hopfield model as a pedagogically rich framework that naturally unifies core topics from the undergraduate physics curriculum and that provides a concise introduction based on concepts such as a model's energy function, dynamics, and pattern stability. We discuss practical aspects of

items.summary: Abstract Exposure to maltreatment in childhood is posited to profoundly disrupt brain development with adverse consequences for cognitive development and health across the lifespan. Here we use “brain charts” from the largest available neuroimaging database to quantify individual brain volumes relative to normative brain growth distributions in 299 children, aged 3 to 13 years, including 123 children with clinically verified maltreatment exposure. Using magnetic resonance imaging, we obtain volumes of cortical grey, total white, and subcortical grey matter and derive chart-based centiles for e

items.title: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline and drug-induced encephalopathy secondary to teprotumumab for thyroid eye disease: a case report and narrative literature review
items.summary: Background Teprotumumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R), is an approved targeted therapy for thyroid eye disease (TED). Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is an extremely rare but potentially severe central nervous system adverse event, with only three cases reported globally to date. items.summary: Abstract Advanced brain age relative to chronological age may predict cognitive decline in healthy aging, but prospective evidence remains limited. Participants with structural MRI and neuropsychological data were included cross-sectionally ( n = 4,606); mean age 76.4y; 58% female) and longitudinally ( n = 2,561; mean follow-up 5.2y). sections.title: Research News
sections.description: Brain and neuroscience related research news from configured RSS feeds.

items.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
items.summary: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions.

items.title: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
items.summary: Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century-old theories and modern neuroscience, suggesting that the brain’s constant predictions shape how we experience reality. The findings could help explain why harmful thought patterns are so difficult to break and offer new insights into treating mental disorders.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
items.summary: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.

items.title: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
items.summary: A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
items.summary: Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.

items.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable
items.summary: The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

items.title: Scientists find a way to fight Alzheimer’s brain damage without removing toxic tau
items.summary: Scientists have found a promising way to protect the brain from Alzheimer’s-related damage by blocking immune cells that contribute to the destruction of neurons. In mice, the treatment preserved roughly 40% more tissue in memory centers and improved memory, even without removing harmful tau protein buildup.

items.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
items.summary: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.

items.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
items.summary: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

items.title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
items.summary: A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

items.title: "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment.

items.title: Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt
items.summary: Eating too much salt may do more than raise blood pressure. It could also harm memory and social behavior. In a new study, Japanese researchers discovered that a soy-derived compound called LPC70 helped protect mice from several damaging effects of a high-salt diet. Mice given the supplement had lower blood pressure, better memory, and improved social interactions compared with mice consuming excess salt alone.

items.title: Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered three brain pathways linked to lasting improvements in people receiving deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-resistant depression. They also discovered that patients who failed to improve after two years shared a striking pattern: insufficient stimulation of a crucial brain connection. The findings suggest that millimeters in electrode placement could make a major difference in treatment outcomes.

items.title: Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a protein linked to youth helps protect the brain’s immune cells from age-related decline. Restoring the protein in older mice improved the cells’ ability to clear debris and reduced signs of inflammation, raising hopes for future treatments targeting brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease.

items.title: Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.

items.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

items.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
items.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

items.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
items.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

items.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
items.summary: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.

items.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
items.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

items.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.

items.title: After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease
items.summary: The FDA has approved the first drug that directly targets Alexander disease, a devastating neurological disorder affecting fewer than one in a million people. Developed through decades of research, Zanvastro showed promising results in clinical trials, stabilizing motor function and even improving movement in some patients.

items.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
items.summary: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

items.title: Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
items.summary: Blocking a receptor called P2X7 significantly reduced inflammation in human brain tissue, revealing a potential new treatment strategy for neurological and psychiatric disorders. The discovery could help researchers repurpose existing drugs for conditions including traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, depression, and schizophrenia.

items.title: What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
items.summary: Cannabinoids may intensify anxiety by removing a natural brake on specific neurons in the brain’s fear center, particularly during stressful situations. In mice, shutting down those neurons sharply reduced cannabinoid-related anxious behavior.

items.title: Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick
items.summary: Stimulating the vagus nerve after practice helped mice develop stronger long-term motor learning, revealing a potentially important window when the brain is still locking in a new skill. The effect was linked to rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, hinting that body-to-brain signals may help prepare the brain for lasting change.

items.title: Your gut bacteria may reveal how fast your brain is aging
items.summary: A UCLA study links faster brain aging to specific gut bacteria and chemical byproducts, with older-looking brains also associated with poorer memory, focus, and mood. The findings suggest that biological signs of brain aging may appear decades before obvious symptoms and could eventually make the gut a target for prevention.

items.title: Your gut may be making a molecule that raises Alzheimer’s risk
items.summary: Scientists have linked a gut bacterial compound called ImP to greater Alzheimer’s risk, harmful brain protein buildup, and faster cognitive decline. The finding raises the possibility that reducing ImP in the blood could one day help slow or prevent dementia.

items.title: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
items.summary: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

items.title: Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may have a reversible weakness
items.summary: The Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may actively damage brain blood vessels and sabotage the cellular systems that remove harmful proteins. Researchers were able to reverse some of these effects in experiments, revealing promising new targets for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and other neurodegenerative diseases.
